title: TINDY ARCHITECTURE OVERVIEW
content:
Tindy helps users find projects and teammates, manage profiles, apply to projects and communicate with other members. This workshop deploys its AWS frontend, backend, database and PDF scanning infrastructure through six CloudFormation templates.
Objectives Deploy stacks in dependency order, use stack Outputs as subsequent inputs, provision a Fresh database, run bootstrap/migration/seed tasks and verify the application through CloudFront. Seeded data supports the login, project discovery, application and review demonstration.
System architecture The diagram shows the arrangement of service groups and application components.
Component Role CloudFront and frontend S3 Deliver the frontend over HTTPS using Origin Access Control for bucket access. CloudFront VPC Origin and internal ALB Route backend requests from CloudFront to the ECS API. ECS Fargate Run the API and one-off database preparation tasks. RDS PostgreSQL Store application data in private DB subnets with TLS connections. Media S3 Store uploads under application prefixes. GuardDuty, EventBridge and SQS Scan PDFs and deliver results to the API worker, with a DLQ for failed processing. Secrets Manager and SSM Store application secrets and Data Protection keys. ECR and GitHub OIDC Store backend images and support GitHub Actions authentication to AWS. CloudWatch and SNS Provide logs, alarms and email notifications. CloudFormation templates Template Scope foundation.yaml S3, ECR, secrets, OIDC and conditional deployment/operations roles. network.yaml VPC, subnets, routes and security groups. database.yaml RDS instance, subnet group and parameter group. integrations.yaml GuardDuty plan, EventBridge rule, SQS/DLQ, SNS and alarms. edge.yaml CloudFront, Origin Access Control, frontend bucket policy and maintenance routing. runtime.yaml ECS, internal ALB, VPC Origin, IAM roles and task definitions. Practical deployment sequence Clean up the existing environment, documented in section 5.7. Import retained Foundation resources, restore the main template and create Network in section 5.3. Create the Fresh Database and Integrations in section 5.4. Create Edge maintenance to obtain its hostname, provision Runtime with DesiredCount 0, prepare and seed the database, enable the API and switch Edge live in section 5.5. Verify and demonstrate the application in section 5.6. This session uses the existing account in us-east-1, a new CloudFront hostname and newly seeded demo data. Deployment pages record verified results and screenshots as execution proceeds.

title: Event 1
content:
AWS CLOUD AND AI DAY HANOI 2026 Date: Tuesday, September 29, 2026 Main Event Location: JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi, Vietnam Organizer: Amazon Web Services (AWS) Participation Format: HCMC Watch Party organized by First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) in Ho Chi Minh City Role: Watch Party Attendee 1. Event Introduction and Objectives AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 was a technology event focusing on Cloud Computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI), Data Analytics, and modern application development.
The event brought together AWS experts, engineers, solution architects, and business representatives to share their knowledge, experiences, and practical technology solutions.
The main objectives of the event included:
Exploring the latest trends in Cloud Computing and AI. Understanding how AI can support software development and workflow automation. Learning about AWS solutions for data management, security, and resource optimization. Gaining insights into building, deploying, and operating cloud-based systems. Creating opportunities to learn from and connect with the technology community. I participated in the event through the HCMC Watch Party, organized by the First Cloud AI Journey community in Ho Chi Minh City, where attendees followed the live broadcast from Hanoi.
2. Keynote Speakers The keynote sessions featured speakers from government organizations, AWS, and leading businesses.
Speaker Position Hoàng Minh Deputy Minister of Science and Technology Jennifer Wicks U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam Dr. Werner Vogels Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Amazon.com Eric Yeo AWS Country General Manager for Malaysia, Vietnam, and Indochina Mai Le Director of Product Management, Katalon Dr. Jens Lottner Chief Executive Officer, Techcombank The speakers shared their perspectives on the development of Cloud Computing, the growing importance of AI, and how businesses can apply technology to solve real-world challenges.
3. Event Schedule and Main Activities The main event in Hanoi took place throughout the day, featuring keynote presentations, technical sessions, hands-on activities, and networking opportunities.
Time Activity 07:30 Registration and Exhibition Opening 09:00 Opening Keynote 10:15 Break and Networking 11:00 Morning Technical Sessions 12:05 Lunch Break and Exhibition 13:10 Early Afternoon Technical Sessions 14:50 Break 15:20 Late Afternoon Technical Sessions 17:00 Event Closing Note: This was the general schedule of the main event in Hanoi, not the complete schedule of the HCMC Watch Party.
4. Key Topics and Highlights 4.1. Keynote – What Does It Take to Solve Problems Everyone Says Are Impossible? The opening keynote explored how technology can help individuals and businesses address challenges that may initially seem impossible to solve.
Key highlights:
Using AI Agents to support daily tasks and software development. Modernizing existing systems through Cloud Computing. Building scalable and reliable applications. Ensuring security and reliability when deploying cloud-based solutions. What I learned:
This session helped me understand that Cloud Computing and AI are not separate technologies. When combined, they can improve productivity, support innovation, and make business operations more efficient.
4.2. Building Software Like Never Before with Agentic AI Time: 11:00 Presenter: AWS Format: A session was available for the HCMC Watch Party. This was one of the topics that interested me the most because it was directly related to software development.
The session introduced Agentic AI, which refers to AI systems capable of carrying out tasks based on specific goals rather than simply responding to questions like traditional chatbots.
Main discussion points:
How AI Agents can assist developers throughout the software development process. Automating repetitive tasks such as code generation, testing, and information processing. Integrating AI Agents into existing development workflows. Understanding important considerations when applying AI to real-world projects. What I learned:
I gained a better understanding of how AI can become a useful assistant for software developers.
However, developers still need to review AI-generated results, monitor system behavior, and make important decisions.
4.3. From Demo to Deployment: Solving Agentic AI’s Toughest Challenges Presenters: Katalon and AWS This topic focused on the challenges of transforming an AI application from an experimental demonstration into a system that can operate effectively in real-world environments.
Key challenges discussed:
Maintaining system stability and reliability. Evaluating the accuracy of AI-generated results. Protecting sensitive data and managing access permissions. Monitoring and controlling AI Agent activities. What I learned:
Building an AI application that works in a demonstration is only the first step.
For long-term use, the application must also be tested carefully, secured properly, and equipped with mechanisms to handle errors and unexpected situations.
4.4. Data Analytics and Building a Data Foundation for AI Another important area covered during the event was data management and how organizations can use data to develop AI applications.
Featured topics:
Build an AI-ready Data Foundation: Preparing and organizing data for AI applications. Data-Driven AI Agents for FSI: Applying data-driven AI Agents in financial services. Amazon Quick Suite: Supporting information retrieval and analysis across multiple data sources. VPBank’s Cloud Journey with Amazon Redshift: Sharing how VPBank developed its data platform using AWS. Key highlights:
Organizing and managing data before using it in AI systems. Connecting information from different platforms and systems. Using AWS services for data storage and analytics. Understanding how data supports better business decisions. What I learned:
I realized that data plays a fundamental role in the development of AI applications.
If data is inaccurate, incomplete, or poorly organized, the results generated by AI systems may also be unreliable.
Therefore, building a strong data foundation is an important step before developing advanced AI solutions.
4.5. Modernizing Applications on AWS The event also introduced solutions that help organizations modernize their existing software systems and improve application performance.
Featured topics:
Amazon EKS: Managing and deploying containerized applications. Migrating a NestJS App from EC2 to EKS with GitOps: Exploring the migration of a NestJS application from Amazon EC2 to Amazon EKS. From Monolith to Microservices: Transforming traditional monolithic applications into smaller, independent services. AWS Transform: Using AI to support the modernization of .NET and SQL Server applications. What I learned:
These topics helped me understand how businesses improve their systems to make deployment, maintenance, and scaling more manageable.
I also learned that not every application requires a complex architecture.
Choosing the right solution should depend on the actual requirements, size, and development goals of the project.
4.6. Cloud Security and AWS Cost Optimization Besides AI and application development, the event also highlighted the importance of security and cost management when using AWS.
Featured topics:
AWS Security Agent: Supporting the identification and resolution of security issues during application development. Workload Identity: Managing application identities and access permissions on AWS. Amazon S3 Storage Classes: Selecting suitable storage options to optimize costs. Amazon Bedrock Cost Control: Monitoring and managing the costs of AI services. Multi-Agent Infrastructure Management: Using AI Agents to assist with infrastructure configuration and management. Key lessons:
Applying appropriate access permissions based on user and application requirements. Protecting data and applications deployed in cloud environments. Selecting storage services based on how frequently data is accessed. Monitoring AWS resources to avoid unnecessary expenses. What I learned:
When developing an application on AWS, ensuring that the system functions correctly is not enough.
Security, performance, resource management, and operating costs must also be considered throughout the development and deployment process.
5. My Experience at the HCMC Watch Party I attended AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 through the HCMC Watch Party organized by the First Cloud AI Journey community in Ho Chi Minh City.
Through the live broadcast from Hanoi, I had the opportunity to follow presentations about Cloud Computing, Artificial Intelligence, and practical technology solutions.
Among the topics presented, I was particularly interested in:
Software development using AI Agents. Data management and analytics. Modern application deployment on AWS. Cloud security and cost optimization. Participating in the Watch Party allowed me to explore knowledge beyond my university courses and gain a more practical understanding of the technologies being adopted by businesses.
It was also an opportunity to learn more about the AWS ecosystem and identify the technical skills that I should continue developing.
6. Knowledge and Skills Gained After attending the event and reviewing the topics introduced, I gained several valuable insights.
6.1. A Better Understanding of Cloud Computing I developed a clearer understanding of how AWS supports the deployment, storage, and management of applications.
Cloud Computing provides organizations with flexible options for building and scaling systems according to their needs.
6.2. Understanding the Role of AI Agents I learned that AI Agents can support different stages of software development, including coding, testing, and workflow automation.
However, AI-generated results still require human supervision, verification, and appropriate access control to reduce errors.
6.3. Recognizing the Importance of Data I understood that data quality, data sources, and data organization are essential when building AI applications.
A reliable data foundation directly contributes to the accuracy and effectiveness of AI systems.
6.4. Increasing My Awareness of Cloud Security The event helped me recognize that security should not be considered only after an application has been completed.
Instead, security practices should be integrated into the system design, development, and deployment processes.
6.5. Understanding AWS Cost Management I learned that using AWS services requires careful resource monitoring and cost management.
Choosing suitable configurations and tracking service usage can help avoid unnecessary expenses.
7. Future Learning and Practical Applications The knowledge gained from the event provided me with a clearer direction for continuing my studies and hands-on practice with AWS.
In the future, I plan to focus on the following AWS services and technical areas:
Amazon S3: Practicing data storage and management. Amazon Bedrock: Learning how to integrate AI capabilities into applications. Amazon ECS and AWS Fargate: Exploring cloud-based application deployment. AWS Security: Understanding access management and data protection. AWS Cost Management: Monitoring cloud resources and controlling operational costs. I also want to apply these concepts to practical projects, especially applications that combine Cloud Computing, Artificial Intelligence, and data processing.
Through hands-on exercises and small projects, I hope to strengthen my technical foundation and gain more experience working with AWS services.
8. Personal Reflection AWS Cloud and AI Day Hanoi 2026 was a valuable learning experience for me.
Although I participated remotely through the HCMC Watch Party in Ho Chi Minh City, I still had the opportunity to explore a wide range of technology topics and learn about solutions being applied in real-world environments.
The topics that impressed me the most were the potential of AI Agents in software development and the role of AWS in building, deploying, and operating modern applications.
The event helped me expand my knowledge, better understand the technical skills I need to develop, and become more motivated to continue learning and practicing AWS.
Overall, this experience encouraged me to explore Cloud Computing and AI more deeply and apply what I have learned to future projects.

title: Blog 1
content:
SQS + LAMBDA: PARTIAL BATCH RESPONSE, DEAD-LETTER QUEUES AND THE SNOWBALL ANTI-PATTERN This article was prepared to be shared with the AWS Study Group community.
Facebook Post: View on Facebook – AWS Study Group VN
Introduction When AWS Lambda processes messages from Amazon SQS, a single failed message can cause the entire batch to be retried. This may result in duplicate processing, unnecessary costs and increased log volume.
This article summarizes AWS documentation and introduces best practices for reliable and cost-effective message processing.
Figure 1. SQS and Lambda architecture with Partial Batch Response, DLQ, CloudWatch and SNS.
1. Partial Batch Response By default, when a Lambda invocation fails, the entire batch of SQS messages becomes available for retry after the visibility timeout.
Enabling ReportBatchItemFailures allows Lambda to report individual failed messages instead of retrying the entire batch.
Key benefits:
Reduce unnecessary message processing. Minimize duplicate operations. Reduce execution and logging costs. Improve processing efficiency. Applications should also implement idempotency because SQS messages may still be delivered more than once.
2. Dead-Letter Queue and Snowball Anti-pattern Without a Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ), failed messages may be repeatedly returned to the source queue. Over time, these messages can consume processing resources and increase costs. This is known as the snowball anti-pattern.
AWS recommends configuring a DLQ through the SQS source queue’s redrive policy.
Configuration Recommended starting point Visibility timeout At least 6 times the Lambda timeout, plus the batching window if used maxReceiveCount At least 5 Dead-Letter Queue Enabled DLQ monitoring CloudWatch Alarm and SNS Failed messages can be investigated and redriven after the underlying issue has been resolved.
3. Provisioned Mode On November 14, 2025, AWS introduced Provisioned Mode for SQS event source mappings.
According to AWS, this feature provides:
Up to 3 times faster scaling. Up to 16 times higher concurrency. Support for up to 20,000 concurrent executions. Configurable minimum and maximum event pollers. However, Provisioned Mode introduces additional costs. Small projects should generally use the default mode unless workload measurements justify the upgrade.
4. Monitoring and Cost Optimization Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon SNS can help detect processing failures and control operational costs.
Recommended practices:
Configure a CloudWatch alarm when the DLQ contains messages. Monitor Lambda Errors and Throttles. Track individual failed messages using custom metrics. Configure CloudWatch Logs retention. Log message IDs and error information instead of unnecessary payloads. 5. Deployment Checklist Enable ReportBatchItemFailures. Implement idempotent message processing. Configure an appropriate visibility timeout. Configure a DLQ and redrive policy. Enable CloudWatch monitoring and SNS notifications. Evaluate costs before enabling Provisioned Mode. Conclusion Combining Partial Batch Response, Dead-Letter Queues and CloudWatch monitoring improves the reliability of SQS and Lambda integration while reducing unnecessary processing costs.
For small cloud projects, starting with a simple configuration and gradually optimizing based on actual workload requirements is a practical approach.
References AWS Lambda – Handling errors for an SQS event source AWS – Best practices for implementing partial batch responses AWS re:Post – Retrying valid SQS messages AWS Lambda – Provisioned Mode for SQS event source mapping AWS Compute Blog – SQS event processing with Lambda Provisioned Mode

title: Blog 2
content:
AWS IAM ACCESS ANALYZER – IDENTIFYING UNUSED ACCESS TO STRENGTHEN CLOUD SECURITY Article Content Access management is an important part of securing an AWS environment. Over time, IAM users and roles may accumulate permissions that are no longer necessary, increasing potential security risks.
AWS IAM Access Analyzer helps organizations identify unused access and review permissions granted to IAM identities, as well as access to supported AWS resources. These findings support the Principle of Least Privilege, which recommends granting users and services only the permissions necessary to perform their tasks.
Key Takeaways Unused Access Analysis: Identifies unused IAM roles, access keys, passwords, and permissions within a configured analysis period. Least-Privilege Security: Helps administrators identify permissions that may be broader than necessary. External Access Findings: Detects supported resources whose policies allow access from outside a defined zone of trust. Access Findings: Provides information for administrators to evaluate whether existing access permissions are appropriate. Permission Remediation: Supports reviewing and modifying IAM policies, removing unused credentials, and investigating inactive IAM roles. Continuous Analysis: Helps organizations regularly assess access permissions as AWS resources and configurations change. However, unused access does not necessarily mean that a permission should be removed immediately. Administrators should verify whether it supports infrequent operations, emergency recovery, or other legitimate requirements.
Practical Applications AWS IAM Access Analyzer is useful for organizations managing multiple IAM users, IAM roles, and AWS resources.
For example, a development team may discover an inactive IAM role or permissions that have not been used for several months. After reviewing the findings and verifying application requirements, administrators can adjust access policies to reduce unnecessary privileges.
Regular access reviews help organizations maintain better security control as their cloud environments expand.
Additionally, unused access analysis may incur additional charges. Organizations should review AWS pricing before enabling this feature.
Architecture Diagram Figure 2: IAM Access Analyzer workflow for reviewing unused permissions and improving access security.
The security review process can be summarized as follows:
IAM Users and IAM Roles → IAM Access Analyzer → Review Findings → Verify Access Requirements → Adjust Permissions
This process helps administrators evaluate potentially unnecessary permissions before making changes to IAM policies.

title: Blog 3
content:
AMAZON RDS POINT-IN-TIME RECOVERY – RESTORING DATABASES AFTER ACCIDENTAL DATA LOSS Article Content During application operations, accidental data deletion, incorrect updates, or application errors can affect database integrity and availability. For systems using Amazon RDS, implementing database backup and recovery mechanisms is essential to minimize the impact of these incidents.
Amazon RDS Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR) allows users to restore a database to a specific point in time within the backup retention period. This feature combines Automated Backups and Transaction Logs, helping users recover data to a state before an incident occurred.
Instead of relying only on manual backups, organizations can use PITR to select an appropriate recovery point more flexibly.
Key Takeaways Automated Backups: Amazon RDS automatically creates backups and retains the transaction logs required to support point-in-time database recovery. Backup Retention: For standard RDS DB instances, the automated backup retention period can be configured from 1 to 35 days. Setting the value to 0 disables automated backups. Point-in-Time Recovery: Allows users to select a recovery point within the available recovery window, up to the latest restorable time supported by the system. New Database Instance: PITR creates a new DB instance instead of directly overwriting the existing database. Manual Snapshots: Provide an additional backup and recovery option. Manual snapshots are retained until users explicitly delete them. Recovery Verification: After restoration, administrators should verify data integrity, connection settings, and application functionality before switching to the recovered database. Practical Applications Amazon RDS Point-in-Time Recovery is useful for applications that depend on relational databases, such as e-commerce systems, order management platforms, and business information systems.
For example, an order management application accidentally deletes important records at 10:00 AM. If Automated Backups are enabled and a point before the incident falls within the available recovery window, an administrator can use PITR to create a new DB instance at an appropriate time before the deletion.
After recovery, the operations team can verify the restored data and application configuration before deciding whether to redirect application connections to the new database.
However, PITR does not completely replace backup testing, data retention policies, or disaster recovery planning. Organizations should regularly evaluate recovery capabilities to ensure that critical data remains protected.
Architecture Diagram Figure 3: Amazon RDS Point-in-Time Recovery workflow using automated backups and transaction logs to restore a database.
The database recovery process can be summarized as follows:
Amazon RDS Database → Automated Backups & Transaction Logs → Select Recovery Point → Create New DB Instance → Verify Restored Data
This workflow illustrates how administrators can restore data to an appropriate point in time without directly overwriting the original database instance.
References AWS Documentation – Managing Automated Backups AWS Documentation – Restoring a DB Instance to a Specified Time AWS Documentation – Backup Retention Period AWS Documentation – Backing Up and Restoring Your Amazon RDS DB Instance

title: Proposal
content:
Tindy — An AWS Platform for Finding Projects and Teammates 1. Executive Summary Tindy is a web application that helps students and early-career professionals find projects that fit their skills and availability. Project leads publish openings for specific positions, track applications, and send invitations. Once a candidate is accepted, Tindy updates project membership and the position’s filled seats so both users see the same state.
The proposed demo runs in US East (N. Virginia), us-east-1. CloudFront serves the React frontend from S3 and sends dynamic requests to the ASP.NET Core API on ECS Fargate. The API stores business data in RDS for PostgreSQL. The private media bucket stores documents, while GuardDuty scans PDFs and Amazon Bedrock drafts profile suggestions.
2. Problem and Scope Problem Recruiting information is often spread across chat groups, posts, and forms. Applicants struggle to see which positions are open, which skills they require, and how many hours they expect each week. Leads must ask for the same information again and track applications, invitations, and open seats across channels. Tindy brings this information together for each project and position.
Demo Scope Workflow User action Result in Tindy Build a profile A member completes onboarding and enters skills, preferred role, experience, and availability. Eligible text or CV PDF input can be used to generate a draft. The profile is updated after its owner reviews and saves it. Apply to a position A lead publishes an open position. A member discovers the project, selects a position, and confirms the application. The lead reviews the submission. The submitted application is Pending. Once accepted, the member appears in the project and the position’s filled-seat count increases. Invite a teammate A lead selects a project and position, finds a candidate who has opted in, and sends an invitation. The candidate opens the notification and responds. The invitation is Pending until resolved. When the candidate accepts and the API verifies eligibility, the application creates a membership and updates the seat count. Communicate Members exchange direct messages or join a project conversation where they have permission. Authorized users see new messages in the correct conversation. Operate the demo The operator releases the frontend and API, checks service health, backs up data, and rebuilds the environment if needed. Release details, verification results, and backup references support recovery. Interpreting Match Scores The API scores each position using four base weights: required skills 40%, preferred role 30%, availability 20%, and optional skills 10%. If a position has no skills in a category or availability cannot be calculated, the API normalizes the remaining applicable weights. A missing preferred role contributes zero for that criterion.
For example, a candidate who matches all required and optional skills and the preferred role, and can contribute 5 of the 10 hours per week the project needs, scores 90/100. The score explains fit. Users make recruitment decisions and the API rechecks permission, project state, and capacity when processing acceptance.
Benefits and How to Evaluate Them For members, discovery exposes the position being recruited for, expected weekly hours, and any missing skills. A profile can be reused across positions. For project leads, applications and invitations are organized by project and position. When recruiting succeeds, the application state, project membership, and filled-seat count can be checked against the same business records.
The trial will measure the value of these workflows. For recruitment, record the steps and elapsed time from selecting a position to both parties confirming its outcome. For profile entry, use the same sample information to compare manual entry with drafting, reviewing, and correcting AI suggestions. Infrastructure cost, demo setup time, and the effort needed to review suggestions inform the evaluation. These measurements support an assessment of value after the trial.
3. Solution Architecture Tindy architecture diagram for the proposal. The numbered walkthrough below reflects the repository configuration and application code.
Step Component Request or data flow 1 Amazon CloudFront and frontend S3 bucket Users open the site over HTTPS. CloudFront serves the React/Vite build from a private S3 bucket. Origin Access Control (OAC) restricts frontend reads to the distribution. 2 CloudFront VPC Origin and Application Load Balancer Dynamic paths such as /api/*, /hubs/*, and sign-in callbacks reach an internal ALB. The web app and API share a hostname, and caching is disabled for these dynamic paths. CloudFront VPC origins 3 Amazon ECS, AWS Fargate, and Amazon ECR ECS runs the ASP.NET Core .NET 10 API container from ECR. The API handles authentication, profiles, discovery, recruitment, and SignalR chat. ALB health checks track task health. 4 Media S3 bucket, GuardDuty, EventBridge, and SQS A private bucket stores media. Certificate and AI input PDFs go through the scanning workflow. EventBridge routes GuardDuty verdicts to SQS so a worker can update document status. A dead-letter queue (DLQ) holds failed messages for investigation. 5 Amazon Bedrock For AI input PDFs, the backend verifies a clean scan verdict for the corresponding S3 object before allowing extraction. Users can also submit text. The backend validates the output and returns draft profile fields, skills, experience, certificates, and warnings for review. 6 Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL PostgreSQL 17 stores structured data such as accounts, profiles, projects, positions, applications, invitations, and messages. RDS uses private subnets, requires TLS, and restricts access through security groups. Three Flows Through the Diagram Application access and data updates (1 → 2 → 3 → 6). The browser loads the frontend from S3 through CloudFront. When users open projects, apply, or connect to chat, CloudFront routes the dynamic request through the VPC origin to the internal ALB. The ALB selects a healthy Fargate task. The API verifies the JWT and permissions for the project or conversation before reading from or writing to PostgreSQL. Web, API, and chat share a hostname.
Certificate upload and PDF checks (3 → 4). The API receives media and writes the PDF to private S3 storage. GuardDuty scans the file, EventBridge routes the verdict to SQS, and a worker matches it with the S3 object or version and updates document status. The API blocks reads or extraction that require a clean verdict while the document is pending or ineligible. The DLQ holds messages that fail processing after the configured retries.
Profile extraction (4 → 5 → 3 → 6). An AI input PDF can proceed to extraction after a clean scan. Users can also submit text directly. The backend calls Bedrock, validates the response, and returns draft profile fields, skills, experience, and certificates. The API writes the selected fields to PostgreSQL after the user reviews, edits, and confirms the save.
Networking and availability. The VPC spans two Availability Zones. The ALB is internal. Fargate tasks use public subnets and receive public IPv4 addresses in the current configuration. Security groups restrict API ingress to the ALB. The demo runbook uses one Fargate task, and the database template configures Single-AZ RDS. The two zones in the diagram show subnet placement. Scaling out requires verification of SignalR across tasks and background event processing.
Security and operations. Frontend assets and media use separate S3 buckets. The backend authenticates users with JWTs and enforces resource-level permissions. Secrets Manager holds connection details and sensitive configuration. GitHub Actions assumes deployment roles through OIDC. CloudWatch collects logs and monitors target health, HTTP 5xx responses, and the DLQ. SNS delivers alerts when notifications are configured.
Components and Design Rationale Layer Responsibility in the demo Why this design fits Web React and Vite produce static assets. CloudFront reads from S3 through Origin Access Control and serves application routes. The frontend can be released independently. Static assets and dynamic session data use separate cache behaviors. API ASP.NET Core runs in ECS Fargate. ECR stores release images. The ALB checks readiness and routes traffic to healthy tasks. The active release can be traced to an image digest, and a new revision can be checked during rollout. Business data RDS for PostgreSQL stores profiles, project relationships, recruitment states, and chat history. Relationships among projects, positions, and members can be checked when the application writes data. Migrations manage schema changes alongside application releases. Files and events The private media bucket stores files. GuardDuty scans PDFs, EventBridge delivers scan events, and the SQS consumer updates document state. Upload and scan completion happen at different times. The queue exposes pending work and the DLQ provides a place to inspect failures. AI When enabled, the backend calls Bedrock and returns a structured draft. Users can compare suggestions with source material. The backend validates profile fields and skill and role mappings before review. Data Boundaries, Access, and Observability Data placement. PostgreSQL stores identities, profiles, project relationships, and workflow states. The frontend S3 bucket contains HTML and static bundles. The media S3 bucket contains file content. A recovery manifest needs both the RDS snapshot reference and the relevant S3 object references so the team can verify that restored records still resolve to the corresponding files.
Access by layer. Security groups govern network access among the ALB, API tasks, and database. The backend authenticates the user and authorizes access to the relevant project, profile, or conversation. The ECS execution role supports startup operations such as pulling the image, initializing logging, and resolving configured secrets. The ECS task role covers AWS actions needed by application code, such as media access, scan-result processing, and AI calls when enabled. The OIDC permissions used by GitHub Actions for releases are managed independently of runtime permissions.
Operational signals. Target health and 5xx responses help narrow down whether a problem is in routing or the application. ECS events and CloudWatch Logs show whether a task could start, stopped, or returned an error. For PDFs, correlate the document state in Tindy with the GuardDuty result and pending SQS or DLQ messages. Recruitment notifications appear in the application through API polling. Chat uses SignalR. SNS serves operational alerts when configured.
Demo Trade-offs and What Would Justify Scaling Decision What the demo prioritizes Evidence needed for a change One Fargate task behind the ALB Keep the always-running footprint small and simplify real-time chat for the demo. Measure traffic and latency. Verify SignalR event delivery across tasks and check that background event processing remains consistent before increasing task count. Single-AZ RDS Keep the starting configuration simple and preserve a documented snapshot recovery path. Define acceptable downtime and data loss. Estimate the cost of Multi-AZ and rehearse recovery before committing to higher availability. API tasks in public subnets with ingress through an internal ALB Use the existing outbound path for integrations. Security groups restrict access to the API. Before moving to private subnets, inventory AWS and external destinations and compare endpoints and outbound paths for connectivity, cost, and operating effort. On-demand AI extraction Process inputs when a user requests a draft and make the run time and cost per attempt measurable. Measure invalid outputs, latency, and token use before considering a background processing queue. 4. Implementation and Testing Prepare the Infrastructure and Data AWS CloudFormation defines six stacks: foundation, network, database, integrations, runtime, and edge. Foundation and network provide buckets, ECR, IAM, and networking. Database provides PostgreSQL. Integrations handles PDF scan results. Runtime deploys the API, ALB, and VPC origin. Edge uses that origin to route dynamic requests once the service is ready.
Choose Fresh to create a database, apply migrations, and seed demo data, or Restore to recover schema and data from a snapshot. For a release that changes the schema, take a snapshot first and run the EF Core migration in a separate ECS task. Verify the running API remains compatible with the migrated schema so the API can return to the previous revision if rollout fails.
Release the Application After CI passes, select the approved commit. Build the backend image, push it to ECR, and record the image digest used in the ECS task definition.
Verify the ECS service is stable and ALB targets are healthy. With the edge in live mode, check that /api/health/ready returns HTTP 200 with status Healthy through CloudFront.
Build the frontend with Vite, publish it to S3, and invalidate the CloudFront cache. Check the home page, login page, and JavaScript bundle through the same hostname.
Run acceptance scenarios with sample accounts and PDFs. Record the commit, image digest, ECS revision, test results, and snapshot ID where applicable. When rebuilding the demo, keep the edge in maintenance mode until the API, database, and required integrations are ready.
Technical and Non-Functional Requirements Release environment. The application uses React/Vite, ASP.NET Core .NET 10, EF Core, and PostgreSQL. Build the frontend to use same-origin API paths. Supply environment settings and sensitive configuration through the deployment workflow and AWS Secrets Manager.
Consistency. Membership admission must use the current project and position state. Check both membership and the position’s filled-seat count after acceptance and reload.
Privacy. Use test accounts and sample documents for demonstrations. Verify permissions when opening a document, requesting an AI draft, or accessing a conversation. Keep references and status evidence in test records. Keep secret values and résumé contents out of those records.
Testability. Prepare test data for successful actions and for rejected actions. Include a position with no open seats, a candidate who has not opted in, a PDF with a pending scan, and a user who lacks conversation access.
Recoverability. Record the relevant snapshot and version before schema changes. Identify a sample set of application records and media files to reconcile after Restore.
Lifecycle Between Demonstrations After a demo, check whether application writes or PDF scan work are still in progress. Once the environment is ready for backup, record the snapshot ID, timestamp, encryption status, API release, and current migration. Confirm that the S3 objects and ECR image needed by that recovery point are retained.
If the environment is taken down between demos, switch CloudFront to maintenance and verify that the distribution hostname is retained. The project runbook defines checks before removing runtime, database, and integrations in dependency order. Preserve the agreed recovery resources, including the snapshot, S3 data, ECR image, and configuration references. At the next demo, select Restore or Fresh based on the goal, verify the database endpoint and health checks, and reopen the edge when the required services are ready.
5. Sprint Plan and Deployment Milestones Tindy development begins on Monday, October 5, 2026 (Week 4). The plan groups Weeks 4–9 into three two-week development sprints. Week 10 (November 16–22, 2026) is reserved for deployment to AWS, post-deployment verification, and completion of the demo.

Set up React/Vite, ASP.NET Core, and PostgreSQL. Build sign-in, onboarding, profiles, and the skill and role catalogs. Sprint 2 · Projects and recruiting Weeks 6–7 · October 19–November 1, 2026 Build project and position management, project discovery, match scoring, applications, teammate discovery, and invitations. Sprint 3 · Integrations and release preparation Weeks 8–9 · November 2–15, 2026 Complete SignalR chat and in-app notifications. Integrate file storage, PDF scanning, and Bedrock profile drafts. Prepare CloudFormation templates, CI/CD configuration, and demo data. A release candidate, test scenarios for core workflows, and reviewed AWS configuration. Sprint 4 · Deployment and completion Week 10 · November 16–22, 2026 Deploy the frontend and API to AWS. Check CloudFront, the ALB, ECS, and RDS. title: Event 2
content:
Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam Date: Friday, October 2, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, VietNam Organizer: AWS Study Group / First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Speaker: Dr. Werner Vogels – Chief Technology Officer (CTO) of Amazon Role: Attendee Event Video: Watch on YouTube Event Objectives Fireside Chat with Dr. Werner: Navigating the Future of Cloud & AI in Vietnam was an online knowledge-sharing session focused on the development of Cloud Computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI), and modern software engineering.
The event provided insights into the history of AWS, the challenges of building large-scale distributed systems, and the changing role of developers in the AI era.
Through the discussion with Dr. Werner Vogels, attendees had the opportunity to learn about cloud architecture, system reliability, AI-assisted software development, and the technical skills required for future engineers.
Key Topics and Knowledge Gained 1. The Origins of AWS and Cloud Computing Economics Dr. Werner Vogels discussed how Amazon’s early challenges in managing large-scale infrastructure contributed to the development of AWS.
As Amazon’s systems grew, traditional infrastructure solutions became increasingly difficult to scale, creating the need for distributed and flexible computing services.
Several important AWS services and concepts were discussed:
Amazon S3: Provides scalable object storage for applications and data. Amazon EC2: Offers virtual computing resources that can be provisioned based on application requirements. Amazon DynamoDB: Provides a managed NoSQL database service designed for scalable applications. Pay-as-you-go Pricing: Allows customers to pay for cloud resources based on usage instead of relying entirely on large upfront infrastructure investments. These developments demonstrated how AWS evolved from solving practical infrastructure challenges into providing cloud services for organizations.
What I learned:
This discussion helped me understand that AWS services were developed to address real-world problems related to scalability, infrastructure management, and operational efficiency.
I also gained a clearer understanding of how cloud computing allows organizations to manage resources more flexibly and control infrastructure costs.
2. Engineering at Scale and System Reliability Another important topic was designing reliable distributed systems that can support large numbers of users while maintaining stable performance.
Dr. Werner Vogels emphasized that system failures are unavoidable, so engineers should design architectures that can recover from unexpected problems.
Several key concepts were introduced:
Tail Latency: Measures the response times experienced by users at the slower end of a system’s performance distribution. High Availability: Ensures that applications and services remain accessible even when individual components fail. Single Points of Failure: Components whose failure can interrupt the entire system. Game Days: Simulated failure scenarios used to evaluate system resilience and recovery processes. Automated Failover: Allows systems to switch to alternative resources when failures occur. These practices help organizations improve the reliability and resilience of large-scale applications.
What I learned:
I learned that building a reliable cloud system requires more than selecting powerful computing resources.
Engineers must also consider failure scenarios, system monitoring, automated recovery, and architectural decisions that minimize service interruptions.
3. The Renaissance Developer in the AI Era The session also explored how Artificial Intelligence is changing software development and the skills developers need to remain effective.
Dr. Werner Vogels introduced the concept of the Renaissance Developer, referring to engineers who combine strong technical knowledge with broader problem-solving and communication skills.
Several important qualities were highlighted:
Continuous Learning: Keeping up with changes in programming languages, cloud technologies, and AI development tools. Systems Thinking: Understanding how different components interact within a complete software system. Communication Skills: Identifying business requirements and explaining technical solutions clearly. Problem-Solving Skills: Evaluating different approaches and selecting appropriate solutions. Ownership: Taking responsibility for software quality, security, and system behavior, including when AI-generated code is used. These qualities help developers adapt to increasingly complex technical environments.
What I learned:
This discussion helped me understand that AI does not eliminate the importance of software engineering fundamentals.
Instead, developers need to strengthen their ability to evaluate solutions, understand system architecture, communicate effectively, and take responsibility for the applications they build.
4. AI-Assisted Development and Responsible Code Review Another topic discussed was how AI tools can support developers throughout the software development process.
AI can accelerate prototyping, generate code suggestions, and help developers explore different implementation approaches.
However, AI-generated results still require careful verification before being used in real applications.
Several important practices were discussed:
Rapid Prototyping: Using AI tools to create initial application designs and test ideas more quickly. Code Review: Examining generated code to identify potential errors and security issues. Risk Assessment: Evaluating software changes based on their potential technical and business impact. Testing and Validation: Checking whether AI-generated solutions meet functional and reliability requirements. Engineering Responsibility: Ensuring developers remain accountable for the software they deliver. What I learned:
I realized that AI tools can improve development efficiency, but their outputs should not be accepted without verification.
Developers must continue to review, test, and evaluate generated code to ensure that applications remain secure, reliable, and suitable for their intended purposes.
Learning Outcomes and Key Takeaways The fireside chat provided valuable insights into Cloud Computing, distributed systems, and the future of software engineering in the AI era.
The main lessons I gained included:
Understanding how AWS developed from real-world challenges involving infrastructure scalability and system performance. Learning about the economic benefits of cloud computing and usage-based resource management. Recognizing the importance of high availability, resilience testing, and automated recovery when designing cloud architectures. Understanding the concept of the Renaissance Developer and the importance of continuous learning, communication, and systems thinking. Learning how AI tools can support rapid prototyping and software development while still requiring code review and testing. Recognizing that developers remain responsible for software quality, security, and reliability when using AI-generated solutions. Overall, the session helped me develop a broader understanding of cloud architecture and the technical responsibilities of software engineers working with AWS and AI technologies.
It also encouraged me to continue improving both my cloud computing knowledge and my ability to evaluate and apply emerging technologies in future software projects.

content:
First Cloud AI Journey – Weekly Meet Up Date & Time: Saturday, October 24, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Organizer: First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Role: In-Person Attendee Event Objectives First Cloud AI Journey – Weekly Meet Up was a technical sharing and networking event for individuals interested in Amazon Web Services (AWS), Cloud Computing, and Artificial Intelligence (AI).
The event focused on practical applications of AI, including building Voice AI systems, managing AWS resources, performing security testing, and using AI Agents to support software development.
List of Speakers Kiệt Trần – Revve AI Long Huỳnh – Styl Solution Thịnh Nguyễn – Styl Solution Xuân An – AWS Student Builder Group HCMUTE Khoa Kiều – Tech Lead, ACB Nghi Danh – AWS Community Builder Key Topics and Highlights 1. Building a Vietnamese Voice AI Call Center The speaker introduced how to build an AI system capable of listening, understanding, and responding through speech using three main stages: Hear – Think – Speak.
Two approaches were discussed:
Speech-to-Speech: Processing spoken input and generating spoken responses directly. ASR–LLM–TTS: Combining Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), a Large Language Model (LLM), and Text-to-Speech (TTS) to process conversations. The most impressive part for me was the demonstration of an AI system conducting a preliminary interview for a Cloud Engineer position in Vietnamese.
This demonstration showed how Voice AI could support recruitment activities and helped me understand the importance of response speed in maintaining a natural conversation.
2. Managing AWS Resources with AWS Resource Access Manager This session introduced how organizations can manage and share resources across multiple AWS accounts using AWS Organizations and AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM).
Main topics included:
AWS RAM: Sharing supported AWS resources across multiple accounts. VPC and Subnet Sharing: Allowing multiple AWS accounts to use shared networking resources. IAM Policies: Managing permissions for users and roles. Service Control Policies (SCPs): Establishing permission boundaries in multi-account environments. Through this session, I gained a better understanding of how businesses organize their cloud infrastructure so that different teams can share resources while maintaining appropriate access control and management.
3. Applying AI to Security Testing The speaker introduced AWS Security Agent, an AI-powered tool designed to support the identification and evaluation of security issues during software development.
Key discussion points:
Reviewing infrastructure configurations written in Terraform. Analyzing source code to identify potential security vulnerabilities. Supporting Pull Request reviews on GitHub and Merge Request reviews on GitLab. Evaluating application security in SIT/UAT environments before production deployment. This session helped me understand the importance of integrating security testing directly into the software development process instead of waiting until the application has been completed.
I also learned how AI can assist developers in identifying potential risks earlier and improving the overall security of their systems.
4. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore This session introduced two important components for building and operating AI Agents using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
AgentCore Runtime: Provides an execution environment for AI Agents and uses MicroVM technology to isolate sessions. AgentCore Memory: Manages information and context that AI Agents need to remember. AgentCore Memory was explained through two main types:

This section introduces three technical blog articles prepared for the AWS Study Group community. The articles focus on storage cost management, access security, and database recovery using AWS services.
Blog 1 - SQS + LAMBDA: PARTIAL BATCH RESPONSE, DEAD-LETTER QUEUES AND THE SNOWBALL ANTI-PATTERN This blog explains how Amazon SQS and AWS Lambda can improve message processing reliability and reduce unnecessary costs through Partial Batch Response and Dead-Letter Queues (DLQs). It also discusses the snowball anti-pattern, Provisioned Mode, and monitoring with Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon SNS, highlighting best practices for handling failed messages and optimizing serverless application performance.
Blog 2 – AWS IAM ACCESS ANALYZER: IDENTIFYING UNUSED ACCESS TO STRENGTHEN CLOUD SECURITY This blog introduces AWS IAM Access Analyzer and its role in identifying unused permissions and reviewing access to AWS resources. It highlights how access findings support the principle of least privilege, helping administrators evaluate IAM policies, reduce unnecessary permissions, and improve security management.
Blog 3 – AMAZON RDS POINT-IN-TIME RECOVERY: RESTORING DATABASES AFTER ACCIDENTAL DATA LOSS This blog explores Amazon RDS Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR), which enables database restoration to a specific point within the available backup retention period. It explains how automated backups and transaction logs support database recovery and emphasizes the importance of verifying restored data before switching applications to a new DB instance.

title: Event 4
content:
First Cloud AI Journey – Weekly Meet Up Date: Saturday, November 14, 2026 Location: 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Organizer: First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Presenters: Members of the First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) team Role: In-Person Attendee Event Objectives First Cloud AI Journey – Weekly Meet Up was a knowledge-sharing and networking event for individuals interested in Amazon Web Services (AWS), Cloud Computing, and Artificial Intelligence (AI).
The event focused on building and deploying AI systems in enterprise environments, covering topics such as cost optimization, AWS resource management, and the development of AI Agent systems capable of collaborating and handling multiple tasks.
Through presentations and practical insights shared by members of the FCAJ community, attendees had the opportunity to learn more about applying AWS and AI technologies to real-world projects.
Key Topics and Knowledge Gained 1. Differences Between AI in Academic Projects and Enterprise Environments In academic environments, AI models are often developed and tested using available datasets with a relatively small number of users.
However, when deployed in enterprise environments, AI systems must support larger workloads, maintain stable performance, and ensure data security.
Several AWS services were introduced during this session:
AWS Lambda: Runs code without requiring developers to manage servers. Auto Scaling: Automatically adjusts computing resources based on workload demands. Load Balancer: Distributes incoming requests across multiple servers to prevent overload. AWS KMS: Helps manage encryption keys to protect sensitive data. AWS IAM: Manages identities and access permissions for AWS resources. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: Helps control AI-generated content and improve safety when using AI applications. These services help AI systems become more scalable, reliable, and suitable for real-world business requirements.
What I learned:
This session helped me understand that building an AI model for a classroom project is different from deploying an AI system in a production environment.
Enterprise AI systems require not only accurate results but also scalability, security, reliability, and effective resource management.
2. Using AI Wisely to Optimize Costs One of the most interesting topics was how to choose appropriate AI models for different tasks instead of using a large AI model for every request.
The FCAJ team illustrated this concept using a restaurant analogy:
Head Chef: A large AI model acts as the coordinator, assigning tasks to other specialized models. Main Course, Dessert, and Cashier: Smaller AI models handle specific tasks at lower costs. Caching: Stores the results of frequently repeated requests to avoid unnecessary processing. By combining larger models with smaller specialized models, AI systems can reduce operational costs while maintaining efficient performance.
What I learned:
I realized that using the most powerful AI model is not always the best solution.
Selecting models based on task complexity and reusing previously generated results can improve response times, reduce costs, and make better use of computing resources.
3. Building Multi-Agent Systems with Strands Agents This session introduced how to combine Strands Agents and FastAPI to develop a Multi-Agent system in which each AI Agent is responsible for a specific task.
Several example Agents were presented:
qa_agent: Uses FAISS to retrieve information from documents and answer questions related to policies. ticket_agent: Handles service requests and includes a human approval mechanism for important actions. research_agent: Uses Tavily to search for and summarize information from the Internet. Instead of requiring a single AI Agent to perform every task, the system distributes requests among specialized Agents.
This approach makes workflows easier to organize, monitor, and expand when necessary.
What I learned:
I gained a better understanding of how Multi-Agent systems work and how different AI Agents can collaborate to complete more complex tasks.
I also learned that dividing responsibilities among Agents can improve system organization and make individual tasks easier to manage.
4. Managing Security and Memory with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Another important topic was managing identities, access permissions, and memory when deploying AI Agent systems.
The following components were introduced:
AgentCore Identity: Supports identity authentication and access management when AI Agents interact with external services. AgentCore Gateway: Provides a way to connect and manage tools and APIs that AI Agents can use. OAuth2 and Amazon Cognito: Support secure authentication and authorization processes. Workload Access Token: Used during authentication and authorization for system workloads. AgentCore Memory: Helps manage information within interaction sessions and retain useful information for future use. What I learned:
This session showed me that developing AI Agents involves much more than generating answers to user questions.
A reliable AI Agent system must also consider security, user authentication, data management, access control, and memory management.
These aspects are especially important when AI Agents are allowed to interact with external services or perform actions on behalf of users.
Learning Outcomes and Key Takeaways The meetup provided valuable technical knowledge and practical insights into Cloud Computing and AI development.
The main lessons I gained included:
Understanding the differences between experimental AI models developed for academic purposes and production AI systems deployed in enterprise environments. Learning how to optimize AI costs by combining large models, smaller specialized models, and caching mechanisms. Understanding how Multi-Agent systems distribute tasks among specialized Agents and manage their activities. Gaining knowledge about authentication, authorization, security, and memory management in AI Agent systems. Learning how different AWS services can work together to create scalable and reliable AI applications. Having the opportunity to exchange ideas and learn from FCAJ community members and other attendees, while exploring AWS and AI solutions that could be applied to the architecture of my internship project. Overall, the event helped me develop a broader understanding of the technical and operational considerations involved in building AI systems for real-world applications.

content:
Connect the deployed stacks into a running Tindy environment. Edge provides the HTTPS hostname. Runtime runs the API behind CloudFront VPC Origin and an internal ALB. Database tasks prepare DB roles, schema and demo data before enabling the API.
Keep Edge in maintenance and Runtime at DesiredCount 0 while preparing secrets, bootstrap, migrations and seed data. Open traffic after successful DB tasks and API health checks.
5.5.1 — Create Edge in maintenance mode Create edge.yaml first to obtain DistributionDomainName, used as Runtime CloudFrontPublicHost and for OAuth callback updates during authentication verification.
Component Purpose CloudFront distribution Provides the HTTPS entry point for frontend and API. Origin Access Control Enables CloudFront access to the frontend S3 origin through its bucket policy. Frontend bucket policy Restricts origin access to the configured distribution. Maintenance routing function Returns HTTP 503 and maintenance JSON for API routes while the backend is being prepared. Initially use EdgeMode = maintenance and leave AlbDnsName and VpcOriginId empty. Switch to live with the new Runtime values after the API becomes healthy.

Resource group Purpose ECS cluster, task definition and service Define the image, configuration, secret references, CPU/memory and task count. Execution and task IAM roles Support container startup and application AWS access. Internal ALB, listener and target group Receive VPC Origin traffic, route requests to the container and check health. CloudFront VPC Origin Connects the distribution to the internal ALB. Security group ingress Restricts ALB access according to CloudFront configuration. CloudWatch log group Records API and database task logs. Conditional one-off task definitions Run bootstrap, migrations and seeding once required parameters are supplied. Create Runtime with a digest-pinned image, DBProvisionMode = Fresh and DesiredCount = 0. Retain the verified OAuth, media and Bedrock text settings. Keep AI PDF false during schema preparation. Once the zero-count service exists, prepare secrets and update parameters to enable DB tasks.

Stable ECS service and Healthy target group. 5 Update alarm dimensions and switch Edge live. title: Workshop
content:
TINDY DEPLOYMENT ON AWS USING CLOUDFORMATION Overview This workshop covers the redeployment of Tindy on AWS using CloudFormation, including setting up a fresh PostgreSQL database, running migrations, seeding demo data, and verifying the application through CloudFront before recording a web demonstration.
The infrastructure uses six CloudFormation templates: foundation.yaml, network.yaml, database.yaml, integrations.yaml, runtime.yaml, and edge.yaml.
Each section includes the deployed resources, required configurations, stack outputs, verification results, and screenshots.
Since Tindy was previously deployed, the workshop begins by cleaning up the existing infrastructure before redeploying all six stacks in the same AWS environment. The new deployment uses a fresh database, demo data, and a new CloudFront hostname.
The cleanup process, documented in Section 5.7, includes maintenance and deletion of all six stacks, each verified with the DELETE_COMPLETE status.

title: SWITCH EDGE TO LIVE
content:

1. Collect Runtime Outputs Open CloudFormation → tindy-runtime → Outputs and copy AlbDnsName and VpcOriginId. AlbDnsName identifies the internal ALB hostname. VpcOriginId identifies the CloudFront VPC Origin created by Runtime. Use the Console copy control, preserve letter case and avoid pasted whitespace. AlbDnsName must contain only the hostname, without a protocol or path.
2. Create the Edge live change set Select tindy-edge → Stack actions → Create a change set. Choose Standard change set → Use existing template → Next and name it tindy-edge-go-live.
Parameter Value Purpose EdgeMode live Enable live API routing configuration in the template. AlbDnsName Copy the matching tindy-runtime Output. Internal ALB hostname for the API origin. VpcOriginId Copy the matching tindy-runtime Output. Connect the origin to the current VPC Origin. FrontendBucketName Keep the existing value. Continue using the existing frontend bucket. Retain current options and create the change set. 📸 Capture filled Parameters and Resource changes at CREATE_COMPLETE / AVAILABLE. Review changes before execution. This milestone confirms only that Outputs have been collected. Live Edge activation remains unverified.
After successful execution in the next stage, verify readiness through HTTPS on the CloudFront hostname. Alarm dimensions, AI PDF, OAuth and frontend deployment remain separate follow-up stages.
3. Recorded change-set preparation screens Standard change set and Use existing template were selected for tindy-edge. The banner mentioning tindy-runtime-start-api refers to the earlier Runtime execution.
The change set name is tindy-edge-go-live. The description retains the existing Edge template description.
The Parameters screenshot records EdgeMode = live, populated AlbDnsName and VpcOriginId, and the retained FrontendBucketName value tindy-foundation-frontendbucket-dxzgxfyg75gu. The ALB hostname has no protocol prefix. Copy both origin inputs verbatim from Runtime Outputs to avoid character transcription errors.
Continue with Next, retain current options, review, then create the change set. 📸 Capture Resource changes at CREATE_COMPLETE and execution status AVAILABLE. Change-set completion and live Edge activation remain unverified at this milestone.
4. Review the live change set Change set tindy-edge-go-live reached CREATE_COMPLETE, Execution status AVAILABLE. It uses a Standard change set, Express mode Disabled and Roll back all stack resources.
Logical ID Action Resource type Replacement EdgeDistribution Modify AWS::CloudFront::Distribution False Exactly one resource changes in place, matching the origin and routing configuration update for live mode. Execution and readiness through CloudFront remain unverified at this milestone.
5. Execute and verify readiness Select Execute change set, retain the configured rollback behavior and Use deletion policy if prompted, then confirm execution. Follow Events to UPDATE_COMPLETE. Check Outputs for EdgeMode = live.
📸 Capture stack UPDATE_COMPLETE and EdgeMode live in Outputs. Once the update completes, run in PowerShell:
curl.exe -i https://d1vcn4g2ifl3k8.cloudfront.net/api/health/ready Expect HTTP 200. 📸 Capture the full HTTP status and response body. If an error is returned, preserve the response and inspect origin configuration and logs before declaring live success. Frontend and OAuth verification follow separately.
